title: Stoic in illness
hook: the leg is hindered, not the will

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was On Anger, Seneca's essay where the first jolt isn't yet anger. Your line was delay the reply.

Day three of the flu. The ceiling has become very familiar. The to-do list on your phone looks like a message from another planet. You feel useless, then guilty for feeling useless, then annoyed at yourself for feeling guilty. Or maybe it's not three days. Maybe it's a back that hasn't worked right for years, or an illness that comes and goes on its own schedule. Epictetus, tradition says, walked with a limp, and Seneca wrote of a long illness in his youth. Both wrote about it from the inside.
screen: `DAY THREE OF THE FLU.` → `USELESS, THEN GUILTY.` → `WRITTEN FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, Epictetus's line. In the Handbook, section nine: illness is a hindrance to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses it. Lameness hinders the leg, not the will. Say that about everything that happens, he says, and you'll find it hinders something else, but not you. Remember who's saying it: a man who, by every ancient account, was lame. Second, the Greek word for will. Prohairesis: the faculty of choosing, your power to judge, decide and respond. For Epictetus it's the part of you that's most truly yours. A fever can take your energy, your plans, your week. It can't make your choices for you. You can still choose patience, honesty, gratitude to whoever brings the soup. Third, Seneca's honesty. In one letter he admits that as a young man he was sick so long he came close to giving up. What held him, he says, was his friends and his studies. He names illness's three burdens: fear, pain, and losing your usual pleasures. He doesn't pretend they're nothing. He just refuses to let them be everything. Fourth, kindness to the body. Being Stoic in illness doesn't mean pushing through or skipping the doctor. The body is not up to you in the end, but caring for it is. Rest, fluids, medicine, a day off without guilt: wise choices, made by a will that isn't sick. The leg is hindered. The will can still choose to be gentle with the leg.
screen: `THE LEG IS HINDERED, NOT THE WILL.` · `PROHAIRESIS: YOUR POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `SENECA: FRIENDS AND STUDIES HELD ME.` · `GENTLE WITH THE BODY.` · then, large: `NOT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: Settle into whatever position is comfortable for your body today, and scan slowly from head to feet, naming any pain, tiredness or stiffness without fighting it: this is the body. Then notice the part of you that's noticing, and say silently, the body is hindered, not the will. Ask the will one kind question: what does this body need from me today?
Prohairesis, Epictetus's word for the will: your power to choose, judge and respond, which illness cannot take from you. Today's word.
Your line: not the will. A fever can take the week, but not the choosing. That's day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet illness by separating what the body suffers from how they choose to respond, while still resting and seeking medical care.
